title: De Ira
author: Lucius Annaeus Seneca
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0255.stoa010.perseus-lat2, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: " Ira," inquit Aristoteles, " necessaria est, nec quicquam sine illa expugnari potest, nisi illa implet animum et spiritum accendit; utendum autem illa est non ut duce sed ut milite." Quod est falsum. Nam si exaudit rationem sequiturque qua ducitur, iam non est ira, cuius proprium est contumacia ;
passages.english: "Anger," says Aristotle, "is necessary, and nothing can be taken by storm without it, unless it fills the mind and kindles the spirit; it must be used, however, not as a commander but as a soldier." This is false. For if it listens to reason and follows where it is led, it is no longer anger, whose distinctive mark is stubbornness;

passages.original: " Non potest," inquit, " fieri " Theophrastus " ut non vir bonus irascatur malis." Isto modo quo melior quisque, hoc iracundior erit; vide ne contra placidior sonitusque affectibus et cui nemo odio sit.
passages.english: "It cannot be," says Theophrastus, "that a good man is not angry at bad men." On that reasoning, the better a man is, the more irascible he will be; consider whether, on the contrary, [he is] calmer and free of passions, and someone who hates no one.
passages.notes: "sonitusque affectibus" appears corrupt; translated as if "solutusque affectibus" ("and free of passions"), the evident sense.

passages.original: Nil minus quam irasci punientem decet, cum eo magis ad emendationem poena proficiat, si iudicio lata est. Inde est, quod Socrates servo ait : " Caederem te, nisi irascerer." Admonitionem servi in tempus sanius distulit, illo tempore se admonuit. Cuius erit tandem temperatus affectus, cum Socrates non sit ausus se irae committere ?
passages.english: Nothing is less fitting for one who punishes than to be angry, since punishment does more toward correction the more it has been imposed with judgment. That is why Socrates said to a slave: "I would beat you, if I were not angry." He put off the slave's correction to a saner time; at that time he corrected himself. Whose passion, then, will ever be under control, when Socrates did not dare to entrust himself to anger?

passages.original: Aristoteles ait affectus quosdam, si quis illis bene utatur, pro armis esse. Quod verum foret, si velut bellica instrumenta sumi deponique possent induentis arbitrio. Haec arma, quae Aristoteles virtuti dat, ipsa per se pugnant, non expectant manum, et habent, non habentur.
passages.english: Aristotle says that certain passions, if one uses them well, serve as weapons. That would be true if, like the instruments of war, they could be taken up and laid down at the will of the one who puts them on. These weapons, which Aristotle gives to virtue, fight by themselves, do not wait for a hand, and they possess rather than are possessed.

passages.original: Hoc semper in omni animadversione servabit, ut sciat alteram adhiberi, ut emendet malos, alteram, ut tollat ; in utroque non praeterita, sed futura intuebitur—nam, ut Plato ait, nemo prudens punit, quia peccatum est, sed ne peccetur ; revocari enim praeterita non possunt, futura prohibentur—, et quos volet nequitiae male cedentis exempla fieri, palam occidet, non tantum ut pereant ipsi, sed ut alios pereundo deterreant.
passages.english: In every punishment he will always observe this: he will know that one kind is applied to reform the wicked, another to remove them; in both he will look not to the past but to the future—for, as Plato says, no wise man punishes because a wrong has been done, but so that wrong may not be done; for the past cannot be called back, but the future is prevented—and those whom he wishes to become examples of wickedness that ends badly he will put to death publicly, not only so that they themselves may perish, but so that by perishing they may deter others.

passages.original: Heraclitus quotiens prodierat et tantum circa se male viventium, immo male pereuntium viderat, flebat, miserebatur omnium, qui sibi laeti felicesque occurrebant, miti animo, sed nimis imbecillo, et ipse inter deplorandos erat. Democritum contra aiunt numquam sine risu in publico fuisse ; adeo nihil illi videbatur senum eorum quae serio gerebantur. Ubi istic irae locus est ? Aut ridenda omnia aut flenda sunt.
passages.english: Whenever Heraclitus had gone out and had seen so many people around him living badly, or rather perishing badly, he wept; he pitied all who met him cheerful and happy—with a gentle mind, but one too weak—and he himself was among those to be lamented. Democritus, on the other hand, they say was never in public without laughing; so little did any of the things done in earnest seem serious to him. Where is there room for anger here? Either everything is to be laughed at or everything wept over.
passages.notes: "senum" is evidently a corruption of "serium" ("serious"); translated accordingly.

passages.original: plurimum potest consuetudo, quae si gravis est, alit vitium. Naturam quidem mutare difficile est, nec licet semel mixta nascentium elementa convertere ; sed in hoc nosse profuit, ut calentibus ingeniis subtrahas vinum, quod pueris Plato negandum putat et ignem vetat igne incitari. Ne cibis quidem implendi sint ; distendentur enim corpora et animi cum corpore tumescent.
passages.english: habit has very great power, and if it is severe, it feeds the fault. To change one's nature is indeed difficult, and it is not possible to alter the elements once mixed at birth; but knowing this has been useful to this extent, that you may withdraw wine from hot-tempered natures—wine which Plato thinks should be denied to boys, and he forbids fire to be stirred up with fire. Nor should they be filled even with food; for their bodies will be distended and their minds will swell along with the body.
passages.notes: "gravis" (severe) may be a corruption of another word (e.g. "gravior" or "prava"); sense uncertain.

passages.original: Apud Platonem educatus puer cum ad parentes relatus vociferantem videret patrem : " Numquam," inquit, " hoc apud Platonem vidi." Non dubito quin citius patrem imitatus sit quam Platonem.
passages.english: A boy who had been brought up in Plato's house, when he was taken back to his parents and saw his father shouting, said: "I never saw this at Plato's." I do not doubt that he imitated his father sooner than Plato.

passages.original: M. Catonem ignorans in balineo quidam percussit imprudens ; quis enim illi sciens faceret iniuriam ? Postea satis facienti Cato : " Non memini," inquit, " me percussum." Melius putavit non agnoscere quam vindicare.
passages.english: Someone in the baths struck Marcus Cato without recognizing him, unawares; for who would knowingly do him an injury? Afterwards, when the man was apologizing, Cato said: "I do not remember being struck." He thought it better not to acknowledge [the insult] than to avenge it.

passages.original: " Ob hoc non cecidit, propter quod alius cecidisset. " Irascor," inquit; "plus faciam quam oportet, libentius faciam ; non sit iste servus in eius potestate qui in sua non est." Aliquis vult irato committi ultionem, cum Plato sibi ipse imperium abrogaverit ? Nihil tibi liceat, dum irasceris. Quare ? Quia vis omnia licere.
passages.english: "For this reason he did not beat [the slave], the very reason for which another would have beaten him. "I am angry," he said; "I would do more than I ought, I would do it more gladly; let this slave not be in the power of one who is not in his own power." Does anyone want vengeance entrusted to an angry man, when Plato revoked his own authority over himself? Let nothing be permitted to you while you are angry. Why? Because you want everything to be permitted.
passages.notes: The opening quotation mark before "Ob hoc" seems misplaced in the edition.
